entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Gospel of Mark is a canonical Christian text attributed to John Mark, who is believed to have been the author or compiler of the Gospel of Luke. Written in the late 1st century AD, it is one of the four Gospels that make up the New Testament and provides an account of the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The Gospel of Mark is significant for its role in shaping Christian theology and its influence on early Christian communities.

The Gospel of Mark contains several key events, including Jesus' baptism by John the Baptist, his temptation in the wilderness, and his healing of a blind man. It also describes Jesus' interactions with various individuals, such as Peter, James, and John, as well as his encounters with crowds and Pharisees.

The Gospel of Mark has had a profound impact on Western Christianity, influencing the development of Christian theology and practices. Its accounts of Jesus' life and teachings have been studied and interpreted by scholars and theologians for centuries.

One notable example of the Gospel of Mark's influence is its role in shaping the concept of 'the witness' in early Christian communities. The Gospel of Mark highlights the importance of eyewitness testimony, emphasizing that only those who had personally witnessed Jesus' life and teachings should be considered authoritative.

In terms of cultural legacy, the Gospel of Mark has played a significant role in shaping Western art and architecture. Its accounts of Jesus' life and teachings have inspired countless works of art, from medieval illuminated manuscripts to modern films and literature.

The Gospel of Mark's significance extends beyond its cultural impact, as it also provides valuable insights into the historical context of early Christianity. Its descriptions of Jewish customs and practices offer a unique window into the religious landscape of the 1st century AD.

It is the shortest of the four Gospels (16 chapters, approximately 11,000 words in Greek) and is characterised by its urgent, fast-paced narrative style — its characteristic Greek word euthys ('immediately') occurs about 40 times — and its focus on the actions and miracles of Jesus rather than on extended teaching discourses.

Scholarly consensus in modern New Testament studies holds that Mark was the first Gospel written (the 'Markan Priority' thesis, developed in the 19th century and now dominant) and that both Matthew and Luke used Mark as a primary source, incorporating approximately 90% of Mark's material while expanding it with additional teaching material (the Q source) and their own special traditions. This relationship — the 'Two-Source Hypothesis' — is the dominant solution to the 'Synoptic Problem' (the question of how the three synoptic Gospels relate to each other). Mark's priority makes it the foundation of the synoptic tradition and the earliest narrative we have of Jesus's life, ministry, death, and resurrection.

The Gospel of Mark opens with John the Baptist and Jesus's baptism (no birth narrative, unlike Matthew and Luke), presents Jesus's Galilean ministry of healing and exorcism, and culminates in the passion narrative — the account of Jesus's final week in Jerusalem, his arrest, trial, crucifixion, and resurrection — which takes up approximately one-third of the entire Gospel.
